1. Core Clinical Tension: A 20-month-old infant presents with hand trauma caused by self-inflicted biting against an abnormally pointed deciduous incisor. The child possesses severe multiorgan congenital pathology: microcephaly, arthrogryposis, ocular and sensorineural auditory defects, perioral hypotonia, and spasticity requiring antispasmodic and anticonvulsant medications. Clinicians must recognize whether this multisystem neuromuscular presentation with arthrogryposis and unique dental dysgenesis (a microdontic primary tooth with thin enamel and a 'claw' cusp) represents a neurogenetic disorder, a metabolic syndrome causing self-mutilation, or a congenital neurotropic viral embryopathy, specifically congenital Zika syndrome.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint concludes immediately following the physical, neuromuscular, and intraoral examinations and baseline low-dose periapical radiography of the primary maxillary teeth, strictly prior to any dental operative intervention (coronoplasty, digital scanning, composite resin fabrication).
3. Differential Distinctions: Other congenital TORCH infections (e.g., CMV, toxoplasmosis, syphilis) cause microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and hearing impairment, but congenital syphilis typically affects permanent dentition (Hutchinson incisors) rather than causing isolated primary incisor claw-cusp malformations, and other TORCH pathogens rarely cause congenital arthrogryposis multiplex. Neurogenetic syndromes associated with self-injury (such as Lesch-Nyhan) were ruled out because the hand trauma was non-compulsive and purely mechanical due to perioral hypotonia and the sharp claw cusp on the abnormal primary incisor.
case_prompt:
A 20-month-old female infant presents to the clinic accompanied by her mother with a chief complaint of traumatic self-injury to both hands caused by a 'pointed tooth.' The child has a complex congenital medical background significant for microcephaly, arthrogryposis, ocular and auditory abnormalities, and neuromuscular spasticity with a seizure disorder managed on chronic anticonvulsant and muscle antispasmodic medications.

On physical examination, the child has microcephaly and joint contractures characteristic of arthrogryposis. Extra-oral and intra-oral examinations demonstrate lip incompetence, hypotonia of the perioral musculature, an upper labial frenum with low insertion, an ogival (high-arched) palate, an anterior open bite, and delayed primary tooth eruption. The deciduous maxillary left central incisor displays markedly abnormal morphology with a sharp, pointed cusp. The remainder of the erupted primary dentition—including the contralateral maxillary incisors, canines, and first and second molars—appears healthy.

A baseline digitally modified periapical radiograph with low radiation dose shows distinct crown malformation of the deciduous maxillary left central incisor compared to the right central incisor, displaying reduced clinical crown height, thinned enamel, reduced mesiodistal diameter, and an abnormal 'claw' cusp, with preserved underlying permanent tooth germs.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Other Congenital TORCH Infections (e.g., Cytomegalovirus, Congenital Syphilis)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although classic TORCH agents cause microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and neurosensory deficits, congenital syphilis characteristically induces permanent incisor notches (Hutchinson teeth) rather than primary incisor claw cusps, and CMV/toxoplasmosis do not classically cause the severe fetal arthrogryposis sequence seen here.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient had microcephaly (Figure 1C), arthrogryposis, ocular and auditory alterations... a deciduous maxillary left central incisor teeth with altered morphology (Figure 1B)... the deciduous maxillary left central incisor had a smaller clinical crown height, thin enamel, smaller mesial diameter, and a "claw" cusp.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Neurogenetic / Metabolic Self-Mutilation Syndromes (e.g., Lesch-Nyhan syndrome)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to involuntary biting and finger trauma in an infant with motor delay and spasticity; however, the self-injury was purely mechanical due to perioral hypotonia resting against a malformed, pointed claw cusp rather than compulsive behavioral automutilation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: chief complaint of self-injury in both hands secondary to a "pointed tooth" (Figures 1A and 1B). The patient had microcephaly (Figure 1C), arthrogryposis, ocular and auditory alterations... hypotonia of the perioral structures

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The constellation of congenital microcephaly, arthrogryposis, ocular and auditory abnormalities, and characteristic primary tooth dysmorphology with claw-cusp malformation confirmed congenital Zika virus syndrome, managed with two-stage digital restorative coronoplasty and indirect composite crowning.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A 20-month-old female patient with ZVCS presented with her mother at the School of Dentistry Clinic with a chief complaint of self-injury in both hands secondary to a "pointed tooth" (Figures 1A and 1B). The patient had microcephaly (Figure 1C), arthrogryposis, ocular and auditory alterations, and a history of anticonvulsant and antispasmodic muscle medication.
